Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic errors in the model forecasts compared to true outcomes.

## Example 1: 2024-09-16
History: Prices have been declining from ~72 to ~64 over 18 days
Model forecasts: Start at 63.69 and gradually increase to ~66.65
True outcomes: Start at 63.21 and continue declining to ~66.97 (wait, that's not matching - let me relook)

Actually looking more carefully:
- Model forecasts the 30d average as starting at 63.69 and ending at 66.65
- True outcomes start at 63.21 and end at 66.97

The model is forecasting more upside than reality. Prices are still declining when model forecasts improvement.

Let me look at the decline more carefully:
- 18-day history: 72.14 → 64.99 (down about 7 points)
- Model 30d forecast: 63.69, 65.24, 65.09, 64.70, 65.68, 66.61, 66.42, 67.83, 69.07, 68.77, 68.25, 66.39, 65.58, 65.82, 65.35, 65.04, 63.38, 64.98
- True outcomes: 63.21, 64.34, 63.70, 62.82, 63.39, 64.10, 63.87, 65.24, 66.52, 66.33, 65.56, 63.61, 62.60, 62.76, 62.05, 61.76, 60.29, 62.01

So the model is forecasting prices that are ~1-3 points too high compared to reality, especially in the early part of the 30-day horizon. The model hasn't fully captured the continued decline.


Sentiment aligns perfectly, with all values being positive. This suggests the model might be overconfident despite underlying price momentum.

I notice a pattern of model forecasts being slightly inflated compared to true outcomes. When prices are declining, the model tends to overestimate future points, particularly in the initial 10-15 day range. The divergence appears most pronounced when sentiment is strong, creating a potential forecasting bias.
